question: Since 2021, democracy in Tunisia has deteriorated significantly1. On 11 February 2023, the Tunisian Government opened an investigation against 17 individuals on a charge of ‘conspiracy against state security’2. Between 11 and 25 February 2023, eight more opposition leaders were arrested by Tunisian security forces on the same charge. Two of those eight, including Chaima Issa, have since been released.
On 24 March 2024, the Financial Times3 reported that the EU was planning to contribute EUR 164.5 million to the Tunisian security forces. 1.

Can the Commission confirm whether or not it – either through direct or indirect management – plans to provide funding to the Tunisian security forces in the coming years, what the exact amount is, and from which budgets this will be funded?

What mechanism has the Commission established to ensure that it does not become complicit in unlawful and politically motivated arrests or detentions, deportations, violence and other human rights violations that have recently been linked to the Tunisian security forces?

How is the EU responding to the continuing arrests of political opponents in Tunisia and the other restrictions placed on them, such as arbitrary travel bans, and what measures are the Commission, the European External Action Service and the EU Delegation taking to secure their unconditional release?
answer: The content and modalities of programmes to be adopted in the coming years under the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe are not yet set. Future programming will be subject to consultations within the Commission services and the European External Action Service, along with European and international partners.

Negotiations with the Tunisian authorities will be part of the process. Robust monitoring systems are in place and are implemented in cooperation with international partners. The Commission monitors its programmes through several means, including regular reports from implementing partners, external evaluation, verification missions and results-oriented monitoring.
Moreover, and depending on the type and content of the action, EU-funded programmes also include the provision of training on international maritime law and human rights.

The EU and Tunisia have a close and longstanding partnership, based on the EU-Tunisia memorandum of understandin g (4) enshrined in a comprehensive Association Agreement (5), which underlines a common attachment to the principles of democracy, the rule of law and human rights.

In this context, the Commission has been closely following the latest developments and recalls the importance of freedom of expression, respect of the right to a fair trial and due process requirements.
